analysis.one_liner: Lets Americans legally import cheaper FDA-approved prescription drugs from Canada and other developed countries.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its committee referral and received no cosponsors before the Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change federal drug law to let pharmacies, wholesalers, and individuals import FDA-approved prescription drugs from Canada and a list of other developed countries, aiming to let Americans buy the same medicines at the lower prices charged abroad. It pairs that with safety measures: registration of importers, licensing of Internet pharmacies, electronic tracking of drugs through the supply chain, and a counterfeit-drug alert network. It was introduced in July 2004, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and never moved further.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay U.S. retail prices for prescription drugs, especially uninsured people and seniors without drug coverage, would gain access to the same medicines bought in Canada and other countries where governments negotiate much lower prices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Americans who pay U.S. drug prices

how_it_helps.text: Lets registered pharmacies, Internet pharmacies, and wholesalers import FDA-approved prescription drugs from Canada and permitted countries like the UK, Australia, and Japan for dispensing in the U.S., with a presumption in favor of importation.

Lets individuals import up to a 90-day personal supply of drugs in their own possession when crossing the border, if bought from a licensed foreign pharmacy with a valid prescription, and gives the Secretary discretion to allow compassionate import of unapproved drugs for continuing treatment of serious conditions.

Creates an Office of Drug Importation Promotion and Safety inside the FDA and requires importers to register, imported drugs to be labeled, and Internet pharmacies to be licensed, with public lists so consumers can identify legitimate sellers.

Requires electronic track-and-trace technology across the drug supply chain and a nationwide network for notifying health professionals and the public about counterfeit drugs, plus strict record-keeping identifying every previous distributor of imported drugs.
Makes websites and advertising services liable if they accept ads from unlicensed Internet pharmacies or ads saying prescription drugs are available without a prescription.

analysis.who_pays: U.S. brand-name drug manufacturers, whose prices are protected by the closed U.S. market, would lose some of the premium they charge American customers. Pharmacies and Internet sellers would take on registration, licensing, labeling, and tracking costs, and the FDA would need a new office and enforcement funding from taxpayers.

drawbacks.text: The Secretary can immediately suspend importation of any drug, dosage form, importer, or even all imports from Canada or a permitted country without judicial review, so the whole system can be switched off by one agency decision.

The bill excludes controlled substances, biologics, many biotechnology products, refrigerated and intravenous drugs, and photoreactive drugs from importation, leaving out exactly the expensive specialty and injectable categories where U.S.-foreign price gaps are often largest.

Opponents argued at the time that importation raises safety risks, because foreign supply chains are harder to police and counterfeit or improperly stored drugs could reach patients despite the bill's labeling and tracking safeguards; the bill itself requires an annual report on whether imported drugs are safe and effective.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The price savings for consumers, particularly uninsured people and seniors paying cash for the same FDA-approved pills sold far cheaper in Canada, are real and would have been immediate for Canadian imports, which the bill makes effective within 30 days of enactment. The safety risks are addressed but not eliminated: the safety machinery depends on the Secretary actually enforcing it, and the suspension authority with no judicial review cuts both ways, able to stop unsafe drugs fast or shut the program down entirely. The exclusion of biologics and most specialty drugs limits how much of a typical patient's bill this helps.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health subcommittee, and it died there when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005 with no committee action, no vote, and no cosponsors.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on July 9, 2004, with no cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day of introduction.
Ten days later it was referred to the committee's Health subcommittee, where it remained.
No further action was taken, and the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, leaving the bill without a committee vote, a floor vote, or a Senate counterpart.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers kept the closed U.S. market that lets them charge Americans the highest drug prices in the developed world, and the congressional committees that defer to the industry's safety arguments faced no political cost for letting the bill die.

for.name: Rep. Chris John
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Drug Importation Promotion and Safety Act and gained no cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; never acted on the bill
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a markup, hearing, or vote after referral, then passed it to the Health subcommittee where it stayed until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew no recorded votes and no cosponsors of either party, so there is no roll-call record of partisan alignment; drug importation cut across party lines in this era, but the source record shows only the Democratic sponsor and committee inaction.

industries.note: Legal importation from Canada and other developed countries would erode the price premium U.S. patients pay for the same FDA-approved drugs, one of the industry's largest and most protected profit sources. The industry's interest is directly the public's cost.

industries.industry: U.S. retail pharmacies and drug wholesalers
industries.note: Pharmacies and wholesalers could legally source lower-cost imported drugs, a potential gain, but must register, label imports, maintain detailed custody records, and adopt electronic tracking systems, and imported inventory competes with their domestic supply.

The bill legitimizes licensed Internet pharmacies selling imported drugs, but imposes a federal licensing regime, inspection and disclosure requirements, return-to-sender rules, and liability for websites and ad services that carry ads from unlicensed sellers, squeezing out the unlicensed operators.
The commingling ban, chain-of-custody records, and counterfeit alert network shut down untracked grey-market channels, targeting the shadow importers whose operations endanger consumers.
